USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain our current tariff and entity-list posture heading into the Osaka G20, while explicitly leaving the door open to resume negotiations with China and signaling we will not trigger the additional ~$300B tariffs or a rare-earth confrontation unless talks definitively fail. Hold the line for now — do not concede unilaterally, but do not escalate further into consumer-goods tariffs or new supply-chain blacklists, because the marginal escalation risk now outweighs the negotiating leverage it would buy. Use the scheduled Trump-Xi G20 meeting as the venue to test Chinese seriousness before raising the stakes again.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real and elevated but not existential. The event timeline shows a sharp May escalation — List 3 tariffs raised to 25% on ~$200B (May 10), China retaliation on its ~$60B list effective June 1, Huawei added to the Entity List (May 16), Google suspending Android/GMS (May 20), and China credibly threatening rare-earth export restrictions plus establishing an 'unreliable entity list' (May 31). This is a genuine material GDP drag with supply-chain and farm-belt exposure, matching the +0.5 anchor: agriculture hit by retaliation (soybeans, with Trump already touting ~$15B in farm aid per web search), and markets flashing recession signals — the 10Y Treasury collapsed from ~2.85% in December to 2.12% and the 2Y to 1.83% as of June 5 (country_health), a steep bull-flattening that prices in growth fear and Fed cuts. That said, US fundamentals are not yet in acute distress — consumer sentiment at ~98, industrial production roughly flat, and Baa credit spreads actually compressed (yield 5.16→4.57) — so this sits at moderate-high, roughly +0.55, not existential. On action: continuing to escalate (the threatened $300B of largely consumer goods) would raise recession risk and invite rare-earth and entity-list retaliation just weeks before the G20, while conceding now would surrender all leverage before Xi has made any matching offer. Given the imminent Trump-Xi meeting and China's refusal so far to meet US demands (per the timeline's May 5 'too slowly' tweet and the broken April talks), the disciplined stance is to hold pressure and keep negotiation open — hence action_score near zero.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain our current retaliatory posture without escalating further, and keep the door open to a negotiated off-ramp at the scheduled G20 meeting with President Trump in late June. Do not unilaterally concede — the US has not made a matching offer, and capitulating on structural reform would threaten core national interests — but equally do not provoke the threatened ~$300B tariff list or deepen the Huawei ban by escalating. Hold the line, signal readiness for talks, and use the G20 window to press for tariff removal and Huawei de-listing rather than doubling down.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high. The US raised List 3 tariffs on ~$200B of our exports to 25% (May 10), threatened 25% tariffs on the remaining ~$300B, and in mid-May placed Huawei and 70 affiliates on the Commerce Department Entity List plus Exec Order 13873 — a direct, firm-level strike at our flagship tech champion and a step toward technological decoupling (timeline 2019-05-10, 05-15, 05-16; Business Insider/LA Times). The macro picture confirms the bite: our exports contracted (Dec 2018 -4.4%, worst in two years), the RMB has depreciated ~8.2% since March 2018, and GDP growth has slowed toward 6.2-6.4%, with PBOC room constrained by debt and capital-outflow risk (Reuters Jan 2019; SCMP; BNP). This sits comfortably at the +0.5 CHN anchor (major export sectors hit, FX pressure, firm-level Huawei targeting) with threats of a broader $300B list above it — hence +0.55, real but not existential given our fiscal/monetary levers and the availability of the G20 off-ramp. On action, escalating further would be self-defeating: it invites the $300B tariff tranche and hardens the tech decoupling, which we can least afford while already facing FX pressure and a slowing export economy. Full concession is equally wrong — the US is demanding structural reform of our development model, a legitimacy issue we cannot concede absent a matched US offer, and we have already retaliated (tariff hikes, unreliable-entity-list announcement, rare-earth signal; timeline 05-13, 05-31, 05-20). A calibrated hold that defends Huawei, avoids feeding the $300B escalation loop, and keeps negotiation alive through the G20 meeting is the proportionate stance.
